item.title: U.S citizen accused of US$165M Ponzi scheme deported from Fiji
item.description: A U.S citizen accused of running an alleged Ponzi scheme worth more than US$165 million has been deported from Fiji to the United States to face federal charges. The U.S Embassy in Fiji confirm Edward Zimbardi was deported on Friday following cooperation between Fiji’s Ministry of Immigration, the Fiji Police Force and U.S. authorities.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S citizen accused of running an alleged Ponzi scheme worth more than US$165 million has been deported from Fiji to the United States to face federal charges.

The U.S Embassy in Fiji confirm Edward Zimbardi was deported on Friday following cooperation between Fiji’s Ministry of Immigration, the Fiji Police Force and U.S. authorities.

Zimbardi faces federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering in connection with the alleged scheme, which reportedly victimised thousands of people.

The U.S Attorney for the Northern District of Georgia, Theodore S. Hertzberg, says Zimbardi allegedly tricked thousands of people into investing in his “Crypto Program” by promising huge returns.

Hertzberg says Zimbardi allegedly used the money for risky currency trades, payments to early investors, a house and expensive vehicles instead.

He says when the alleged scheme collapsed, Zimbardi fled to Fiji in an attempt to evade federal prosecution.

The operation to return Zimbardi to the United States involved the U.S E mbassy in Suva’s Diplomatic Security Service, the United States Department of Justice Office of International Affairs and the FBI.

Hertzberg says, with the assistance of law enforcement and diplomatic authorities in Fiji and the United States, Zimbardi has been returned to th e U.S a nd will face trial.

The U.S Emb assy in Suva has commended the Ministry of Immigration and the Fiji Police Force for their speed and proficiency in handling the case.

The allegations against Zimbardi have not been proven in court.

He will appear in federal court today to face wire fraud and money laundering charges.

item.title: FCEF challenges FTUC $8 living wage petition, calls for evidence-based approach
item.description: The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation says the Fiji Trades Union Congress campaign for an $8-an-hour national living wage must be based on evidence and proper wage-setting processes, rather than the number of signatures collected. FCEF CEO Edward Bernard says while the federation respects FTUC’s democratic right to target 100,000 signatures for its petition, a petition cannot replace a credib
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation says the Fiji Trades Union Congress campaign for an $8-an-hour national living wage must be based on evidence and proper wage-setting processes, rather than the number of signatures collected.

FCEF CEO Edward Bernard says while the federation respects FTUC’s democratic right to target 100,000 signatures for its petition, a petition cannot replace a credible wage-setting system.

Bernard's comments come following FTUC's $8-an-hour national living wage , which began last week.

Bernard says the issue is not whether workers deserve decent wages, but whether an $8-an-hour rate can be justified through evidence, economic analysis, transparent methodology and genuine tripartite dialogue.

He says a petition can show how many people support an $8 wage, but cannot determine whether Fiji is ready for a living wage or whether $8 is the appropriate benchmark.

Bernard says the International Labour Organisation has set out principles for establishing a living wage, including the use of robust evidence, consultation with workers and employers, transparency and technical validation.

He says the process should also reflect local and regional economic realities before a living wage is introduced through established wage-setting mechanisms.

Bernard says FTUC's proposal of $8 an hour national living wage represents an increase of about 60 percent and notes that the ILO's operationalisation principles refer to incremental progression from minimum wages towards living wages.

item.title: Coconut sellers issued notices for illegal dumping along Naivorovoro Road in Nakasi

item.content:encoded:
Concerns over illegal dumping by coconut sellers along Naivorovoro Road in Nakasi have prompted the Nausori Town Council to take action, with the council saying notices have been issued and the matter has been referred to Police.

Concerned resident Shom Jeet informed fijivillage News this morning that coconut waste and other rubbish are being dumped in the drains and along the roadside near Saint Joseph the Worker Primary School, causing the rubbish to continue accumulating.

He also alleges that some coconut sellers harass drivers and members of the public into buying coconuts , at times moving in front of vehicles to slow them down in an attempt to make sales.

Responding to our questions, Nausori Town Council CEO Rajesh Kumar says the council has been removing the rubbish and will continue collecting waste from the area.

Kumar says he has personally visited the area and confirms that coconut sellers have been illegally dumping waste.

He says the matter has been referred to Police and the sellers have already been issued notices.

Kumar says he has also personally assured the complainants that the council is aware of the issue and that the rubbish is being collected.

He says the council will continue to monitor the area and take the necessary action.

item.title: Australia pledges to defend Fiji under Veitacini Treaty
item.description: Australia says it will come to Fiji’s aid and defend the country if Fiji comes under attack under the newly signed Veitacini Treaty, which establishes an alliance between the two countries. Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts says the agreement represents the deepest level of commitment and demonstrates the level of trust bet
item.content:encoded:
Australia says it will come to Fiji’s aid and defend the country if Fiji comes under attack under the newly signed Veitacini Treaty, which establishes an alliance between the two countries.

Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts says the agreement represents the deepest level of commitment and demonstrates the level of trust between Fiji and Australia.

When questioned on Article 6 of the treaty, which deals with mutual defence, Roberts says Fiji and Australia have committed to coming to each other’s aid if either country faces an external threat or attack, following consultation between the two countries.

Insert: We'll be there for each other KK 17th Aug

He says while the commitment is significant, the relationship feels natural given the long history between the two countries, including Fijians and Australians serving alongside each other in wars and peacekeeping operations.

The High Commissioner says the treaty also includes commitments to democratic processes and provides a framework for the two countries’ militaries to work more closely together.

He says Fiji and Australia already have significant defence cooperation, with about 150 Fijian troops recently returning from exercises in Australia as part of what has become an annual arrangement.

Roberts says senior Fijian military officers also undertake advanced training in Australia, while officers from the two countries are embedded within each other’s forces, which demonstrates a high level of trust between the two countries.

When asked whether the treaty could apply in the event of a political takeover or coup in Fiji, Roberts says an alliance generally deals with external threats.

However, he says the treaty contains a commitment by both countries to democratic processes and that the Fiji-Australia partnership is based on common values, including democracy.

He adds the treaty is also described as the Ocean of Peace Alliance, reflecting Fiji and Australia’s desire for a safe and peaceful Pacific.

He adds both countries want regional security challenges to be addressed in the Pacific way and within the Pacific family which aligns with Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s Ocean of Peace concept and the broader regional approach discussed by Pacific Islands Forum leaders.

Roberts says Australia and Fiji have previously demonstrated their ability to respond together to regional security challenges, including peacekeeping efforts in Bougainville and the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands.

He says the two new agreements also demonstrate how important Australia considers its partnership with Fiji and its commitment to the security and prosperity of the Pacific.
